seo.title: Karmic tail 9 18 18 compatibility: The Hermit and two Moons
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 18 18 compatibility: what The Hermit and two Moons mean in a couple's tail, a middle no personal chart has, and the key in Pushkin's Snowstorm.

title: The 9-18-18 karmic tail in compatibility: one secret shared by two
short: Three cards, and two of them are the same: The Hermit, The Moon, The Moon. And the middle is one that a personal chart can never have. In compatibility, the 9-18-18 tail is the story of two people who come together over silence, pass through a fog of guesses and learn one main thing: to say out loud what each of them keeps to themselves. The secret of this tail is that the thing each partner guards as a wall between them often turns out to be shared.

sections.h2: A middle that no personal chart can have
paragraphs: The first clue is arithmetic. In a personal chart nobody chooses the middle of the tail: it is the sum of the two outer numbers. An entry of 9 and a task of 18 would give 9 + 18 = 27 → 9, and the tail would come out as 9-9-18. The couple's middle is different: 18. It is not derived from the outer numbers. Every point of a couple's chart is the sum of the matching points of the two personal charts, so the couple's middle is the sum of the partners' middles. The Moon in the middle is something the two people bring with them.

Most often they bring the same pattern. In 65% of couples with the 9-18-18 tail, both partners have the same personal tail, 18-9-9. Another 23% come from the combination 18-3-12 with 9-15-6, 9% from 18-6-15 with 9-12-3, and 2% each from two rare combinations with no 9s or 18s at all (15-8-11 with 21-10-7, and 21-4-10 with 6-14-8). The tail itself occurs in roughly one couple in 81 (1.228%) and ranks 27th of the 97 couple tails.

In the main case the numbers perform a swap. The personal tail 18-9-9 begins with The Moon and continues with The Hermit. Add two such tails together and the two Moons give The Hermit at the couple's entry (18 + 18 = 36 → 9), while the two Hermits give The Moon in the middle and in the main task (9 + 9 = 18). This is not a reading of the personal tails, which have roles of their own; it is simply how the numbers add up. But the picture is striking: what each partner brings as their own Moon becomes the couple's shared quiet, and what each brings as their own quiet becomes the couple's shared fog.

Hence the first guess about the plot. This couple is often made of two people who carry the same thing. There is a story in which two people carry not just a similar pattern but one and the same secret, and do not know it.

sections.h2: The Snowstorm: a wedding at which nobody saw a face
paragraphs: Pushkin finished The Snowstorm (Metel) on 20 October 1830 at Boldino. He was engaged and cut off from his fiancée by cholera quarantines; in a letter to her he complained, in French, that their marriage seemed always to be fleeing before him. The story he wrote that autumn is about a wedding the bridegroom cannot reach.

The end of 1811. Seventeen-year-old Maria Gavrilovna, who, as Pushkin puts it in T. Keane's 1916 translation, "had been brought up on French novels, and consequently was in love", agrees with Vladimir, a poor sub-lieutenant, to marry him secretly in the church of a nearby village. On the night of the elopement a snowstorm rises. The bride is driven to the church, while the bridegroom circles the fields all night and at dawn finds the church locked.

In the morning Masha comes down to tea as if nothing had happened, and that night she falls into a fever. Her parents decide that fate cannot be escaped and consent to the marriage, but they receive "a half-insane letter" from Vladimir: he joins the army, is badly wounded at Borodino and dies in Moscow. Masha turns down every suitor and keeps his books and drawings. Some years later a wounded colonel of the Hussars, Bourmin, appears in the district: quiet, attentive, silent. They plainly love each other, but he does not propose and she does not hurry him.

The denouement comes by the pond, under a willow. Bourmin declares his love and at once announces "an insurmountable barrier" between them: he has been married for nearly four years and does not know to whom. At the beginning of 1812 a snowstorm led him, an officer passing through, into an unfamiliar village; in the church he was taken for the late bridegroom, and he stood at the altar with a girl he did not know, "impelled by an incomprehensible, unpardonable levity", as he later says. When they were told to kiss, she cried out "Oh! it is not he! it is not he!" and fell senseless. The last words of the story belong to Masha: "My God! my God! <…> then it was you! And you do not recognize me?"
That is the whole secret. For years two people kept one and the same secret from each other. Each believed it was a wall between them, and it was their wedding.

sections.h2: Entry 9: the quiet they meet on
paragraphs: Point M, Entry to the task, is what the couple wants together, what they agree on and what language they speak. The same point also sits in the sphere Relationship and common language. In 9-18-18 it holds The Hermit, and Pushkin portrays it more precisely than any handbook. Suitors circle Maria Gavrilovna, "but she gave not the slightest hope to any of them", and when her mother urged her, she "shook her head and became pensive". Bourmin "seemed to be of a quiet and modest disposition", he had "a spirit of decorum and observation", and "whatever she said or did, his soul and eyes followed her". The noisy suitors withdrew. Two people remained, who had recognised each other by their pensiveness.

This is how the couple's entry looks in life, too. From the first meetings both are comfortable being silent side by side. Nobody asks "what are you thinking about?", each has a corner and a time of their own, and love shows in deeds rather than words: a cup of tea made while the other was working, a blanket laid over someone without a word. The unspoken agreement goes something like this: "no prying into each other's souls". For two careful people this is a gift. At last there is someone close who will not break the door down.

But the entry to the task stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. In Pushkin both are held back by silence, and both honestly. Bourmin does not propose because he is married. Maria Gavrilovna does not expect him to, because, as she will say, "I could never be your wife." In Waite's list of divinatory meanings The Hermit opens with the words "Prudence, circumspection". Here they are at their very best, and it is precisely they that hold the wall up. The quiet the couple came together on is the same quiet that keeps them from saying the main thing.

A couple with The Hermit at the entry usually moves slowly, taking its time from the first kiss to the wedding. In Pushkin this order is turned inside out. The wedding took place nearly four years before the first kiss, and the kiss itself stays beyond the last line: in the church Bourmin "was about to kiss her", and it went no further.

sections.h2: Middle 18: each writes a novel about the other
paragraphs: How does the couple travel from the quiet to the task? Pushkin answers in a single sentence: "the silence of the young Hussar excited her curiosity and imagination". That is the passage from 9 to 18. The Hermit is silent; The Moon makes things up.

Maria Gavrilovna goes through the versions like a fortune-teller through cards: "Was it timidity, inseparable from true love, or pride, or the coquetry of a crafty wooer?" and, "after long reflection", settles on timidity. Wrong. Bourmin, too, knows her secret in advance: "I know <…> I know that you once loved, but death and three years of mourning…." Also wrong. Both "know", and both are mistaken. In Wen, The Hermit reversed describes someone who "thinks he or she knows best" and "prefers to rely on his or her own mistakes and experience than to learn from others". There are no reversed cards in the matrix, but the words "I know" in Bourmin's mouth are an exact portrait of this trap: one's own lamp lights up the guess so well that there seems no point in asking.

For Waite The Moon is "life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit", and from the first page Pushkin keeps his heroine in this light: the French novels, the plan to elope that was "very congenial to the romantic imagination of Maria Gavrilovna", the scene by the pond where she awaits the declaration "with a book in her hands, and in a white dress: a veritable heroine of romance". She even lets the conversation drop on purpose to hasten the denouement; Pushkin calls this her voennye deistviya, her "military operations" (Keane softens it to "stratagem"). Among the reversed meanings of The Hermit, Waite lists "policy". This is not deceit but stage direction. Each writes a novel about the other and waits for the other to play their chapter.

Even the neighbours take part. They "spoke about the marriage as if it were a matter already decided upon", or, in Pushkin's Russian, as of "a thing already done", and they were literally right: the wedding had taken place long before, though they had no idea how right they were. Where The Moon is, rumours follow, and rumours are sometimes more accurate than those who spread them think.

The sharpest scene of the middle is the fever. Maria Gavrilovna "divulged her secret during her delirious ravings", but "her words were so disconnected" that her mother understood from them only what she already believed: her daughter was in love with Vladimir. The truth, spoken in a fog, is heard as a familiar story. Living couples do this all the time. What one finally manages to say in tears, in a quarrel or late at night in hints, the other hears as confirmation of a novel they wrote long ago.

In everyday life the middle of 9-18-18 looks like this. She has been quiet for a week. He runs through the explanations: work, tiredness, himself, someone from the past. To ask would break the agreement about not prying, so he does not ask. She notices his coolness and decides he is tired of her. Both behave reasonably, only on invented data. Resentment arrives from a story that never happened, and a quarrel flares up out of nothing.

There is one more detail. In a personal chart the middle lies on the straight road from entry to task: it is their sum. This couple's middle has left the road. In Pushkin both men lose their way. The snowstorm leads Vladimir into the fields, where "earth and sky became confounded", and Bourmin's driver "drove past the place where we should have come out upon the road". What brings Bourmin out of the storm is a light: "I saw a light in the distance, and I ordered the driver to proceed towards it." The middle 18 is not a wrong turn but the route itself: this couple travels to its task off the road, guided by a small light.

sections.h2: Main task 18: "It is not he!" and "Then it was you!"
paragraphs: Point D is the couple's main task, and it is read mostly through its minus: what the two of them fail at and what they need to learn. The minus of The Moon as a task is an image formed at the start and one day collapsing, feelings hidden as if they were weakness, jealousy and resentment aimed at imaginary people. In Pushkin the image is formed quite literally. Bourmin enters "the church, which was feebly lit up by two or three tapers", the bride sits "in a dark corner of the church", and the witnesses "only occupied themselves with her". She expects one face, sees another and cries: "Oh! it is not he! it is not he!"

Nearly four years later the same woman says of the same man: "then it was you!" Between those two exclamations lies the main task of The Moon. The first is the collapse of an image: this is not the one I imagined. The second is recognition: it is you, the real one. A 9-18-18 couple learns to move from the first to the second: not to run away at the moment the image collapses, but to wait until the person shows through it.

Waite's list of divinatory meanings for The Moon ends with the word "error". The whole plot of The Snowstorm is an error, the wrong bridegroom, that turns out to be right. Pushkin even attaches a proverb to it. Deciding to give Masha to Vladimir, her parents console themselves with the saying that "a woman cannot ride away from the man who is destined to be her husband", and the narrator jabs at once: "Moral proverbs are wonderfully useful in those cases where we can invent little in our own justification." The Russian proverb literally says that you cannot ride round your destined one on horseback, and it comes true word for word, only about another man: the destined one arrived by post-horses through the snowstorm, while Vladimir, with his own horse, never got there. That is how The Moon errs. The feeling is real; its address is invented.

The conversation by the pond shows how this tail works. Bourmin: "there still remains a grave duty for me to perform — to reveal to you a terrible secret which will place between us an insurmountable barrier…." Maria Gavrilovna interrupts: "That barrier has always existed." Both are right. The barrier existed, and it was their wedding. What each hid as a wall was the very thing that bound them.

Wen distinguishes two kinds of secret: "The High Priestess suggests secrets that a person is withholding; The Moon represents secrets of the natural world, the hidden condition of the Seeker's situation that will reveal itself in time." The Snowstorm has both. Each kept quiet about their own story: those are High Priestess secrets. But the main thing, that they were husband and wife, neither of them knew: that is The Moon's secret, and it came to light only when both had told their own. In our reading, this is where the secret of 9-18-18 lies. What each partner in such a couple keeps quiet about, an old guilt, the fear of not being who one seems, a story that would supposedly spoil the image, often concerns them both. Once spoken, it does not drive them apart but brings them together: it becomes clear where the two of them really stand.

And Masha's last line is not a statement but a question: "And you do not recognize me?" They had seen each other every day and did not recognise each other, because each was looking at an image: she at the hero of a novel, he at a nameless wife from a dark church. The main task of The Moon in this couple is recognition. To see the living person where one is used to seeing one's own guess.

sections.h2: A mirror, a candle and two places at the table
paragraphs: Pushkin left the key to The Snowstorm right above its first line: an epigraph from Zhukovsky's Svetlana, a ballad about fortune-telling at Yuletide. A table is laid in the girl's room, and on it stand, in our translation, "a mirror with a candle; / two places laid at the table". At midnight the girl looks into the mirror to see her destined bridegroom: "Dark the glass; and all around / deathly silence lies; / with a trembling flame the candle / barely sheds its light…"

The two objects of the fortune-telling are the two cards of this tail. The candle is The Hermit's light, small and its own. The mirror is The Moon's light, reflected. The two places at the table are the couple. And in Svetlana's dream the bridegroom is silent the whole way: "'Why so silent, love?' / Not half a word in reply: / he gazes at the moonlight, / pale and full of gloom" (our translation). These four lines hold the whole of the 9-18-18 tail: a question asked into silence, and a loved one who looks at the moon instead of answering.

For the epigraph Pushkin took the stanzas about the sledge and the lonely church, and where Zhukovsky has a black coffin standing in the middle of the church and "the friend is silent", he put a row of dots. His church in the snowstorm is for a wedding, not a funeral. The ballad itself ends with a moral that suits the story too: "Here misfortune is a lying dream; / happiness, the waking" (our translation).

Pushkin had used the same ballad for an epigraph before, for the fifth chapter of Eugene Onegin, where Tatiana tells her fortune. There are lines in it that could hang over this tail: "She turns a mirror on the moon; / but in the dark glass all alone / the mournful moon is trembling…" (our translation). You look in the mirror for the face of your destined one, and you see the moon. That is how The Moon works in the middle and the task of this couple: looking into the other, each sees reflected light, that is, their own guesses.

sections.h2: The cost: care that becomes a wall
paragraphs: If the couple stays in the middle, the tail shows itself in its minus, and its cost is a quiet one. Nobody shouts or lies. Two decent people simply spend years shielding each other from their secret. Masha turned down every suitor. Bourmin has been married for years without a wife: "I have no hope of ever discovering the woman upon whom I played such a cruel joke." Both live beside an image rather than a person. Tenderness is held back as if it were weakness. Each is sure the other would not understand, and the very agreement about not prying keeps them from finding out.

In her reading of The Moon reversed, Wen makes a hard observation: "The repressed latent will always surface, and any strong intention to repress will cause a violent surfacing." There is no point in this tail waiting for the secret to dissolve on its own. The only question is whether it comes out as a conversation by the pond or as a fever after which the words are "so disconnected".

One caveat. The tail speaks of the careful silence of two equal people. If someone keeps silent out of fear of their partner, because of threats, control or violence, this is no longer a lesson of the tail but a reason to turn to a psychologist or a crisis service, and in danger to call your local emergency number.

sections.h2: The way out: "Continue: I will relate to you afterwards"
paragraphs: The scene by the pond has a moment that is easy to miss. Bourmin begins, Masha interrupts him with her barrier, and he asks her to stop: "be silent, for God's sake, be silent" (our translation). It seems The Hermit has won, and each will keep their own. And then Masha does what turns the whole plot around: "Continue: I will relate to you afterwards.... But continue, I beg of you." She puts her own secret aside in order to hear his to the end. Only because of this does she recognise her story in his.
From this come a few simple practices for a 9-18-18 couple:

ul: **Say a guess as a guess.** Not "you're tired of me", but "I've told myself you're tired of me. Is that true?".
**Don't answer "I know" to what hasn't been said yet.** Bourmin's costliest mistake fits into two words.
**Hear the other person out.** Put your own "but in my case" off until "afterwards".
**Name at least the outline.** "There's something I find hard to talk about" is no longer a wall but a door.

**Announce the silence out loud.** The right to withdraw remains, but with an explanation: "I need some time alone, it's not about you." For The Moon, withdrawing is a way to recover, not a lack of love, and the partner needs to know that.
**Check the image against the person.** From time to time ask yourself what you know about them and what you have made up.

paragraphs: For the resolution of The Moon's confusion Wen has a formula borrowed from Flannery O'Connor: "everything that rises must converge". Two Hermits climb, each their own mountain, and The Moon promises that the roads will meet. In the strong version of this tail the couple loses neither its quiet nor its mystery. It can still be silent side by side, keeps discovering something new in the other year after year and understands the other without words. But its fog is shared, not dividing: the two of them look out of one window, not each into a mirror of their own.

The clearest example is two people born on the same day, 14 September 1975. Their personal charts are identical: day 14, month 9, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22, karmic task 14 + 9 + 22 = 45 → 9, centre 14 + 9 + 22 + 9 = 54 → 9. Each has the personal tail 18-9-9: entry 9 + 9 = 18, middle 18 + 9 = 27 → 9, task 9. The couple's points are added pair by pair:

The middle is not recalculated from the outer numbers: 9 + 18 would give 9, while the couple has 18, the sum of the two personal middles. A couple can see its own tail in the compatibility reading from two dates.

In this couple The Moon also stands in the centre (9 + 9 = 18), in the sphere What to create together, and in the couple's values. This is an extreme case: two identical charts double every point. Across all couples with the 9-18-18 tail, the couple's centre is The Moon in two cases out of three (66.8%) and The Hermit in the rest (33.2%). In the couple's values it is the other way round: more often The Hermit (70.3%), less often The Moon (29.7%). No other arcana appear at these two points in such couples. In a typical couple the fog lives in the atmosphere, and the quiet in what the union exists for.

sections.h2: 18-9-18 and 18-18-9: the same numbers in a different order
paragraphs: The 18-9-18 tail (0.963% of couples, centre almost always The Moon, 91.1%) enters through The Moon: the couple is brought together by mystery, enchantment, a story like a novel. The path runs through The Hermit's quiet, and the task is The Moon again. The 18-18-9 tail (0.221% of couples, centre usually The Hermit, 82%) enters and travels through The Moon, and sets The Hermit as the main task: learning not to hide from each other in a shell while still respecting the other's solitude. In 9-18-18 everything begins with quiet, the fog grows out of it, and the task is to bring it into the light.

ul: **M · Entry to the task — 9, The Hermit.** What the couple wants together: a quiet in which nothing has to be explained, an unhurried pace, respect for the other person's closed door. Glances and pauses are also the language in which the two of them come to terms.
**N · Middle of the task — 18, The Moon.** How the couple travels: through guesswork. Each explains the other's silence with a story of their own, and the stories grow faster than words.

**D · Main task — 18, The Moon.** What to learn: to bring what is hidden into the light, to hear the other person out, and to recognise the living person behind the image that has formed in one's head.

intro: What follows is an investigation: what is written in the numbers themselves, what Waite and Wen say about the cards, and why Pushkin's The Snowstorm explains this tail best of all, living it out from the first line to the last.

faq.q: What does the 9-18-18 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail with The Hermit at the entry to the task and The Moon in the middle and in the main task. The couple comes together over quiet and respect for each other's boundaries, passes through guesses and things left unsaid, and learns to bring what is hidden into the light: to talk about feelings, not to second-guess the other, to check the image of the partner against the partner.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. The tail shows a task, not a verdict: the method gives no compatibility percentages and predicts no events. The strong version of 9-18-18 is a couple that can both be silent side by side and talk, and whose mystery is shared rather than dividing.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the couple's tail 18 and not 9?
faq.a: The couple's points are not derived from the outer numbers: each is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts. The couple's middle is the sum of the partners' middles, most often 9 + 9 = 18. In a personal chart the middle equals the reduced sum of entry and task, 9 + 18 → 9, which is why there is no personal 9-18-18 tail.

faq.q: Can this tail be read through the partners' personal tails?
faq.a: No: a personal tail has different points and different roles. The personal tails only show what the sum was made of. Most often, in 65% of such couples, both partners have the same personal tail, 18-9-9.

faq.q: How do I find my couple's tail?
faq.a: Enter both birth dates into the compatibility calculator. The three numbers appear in the sphere The couple's karmic tail; read them in the order Entry to the task, Middle of the task, Main task.

unit.meaning: Your task is to speak the secret each of you guards as a wall: often it is the very thing that binds you.
